questions.enonce_markdown: Describe an experiment that is used to determine the enthalpy of combustion of ethanol in the laboratory. Your description should end with collection of data. *[16 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Principle:** the heat given out when a known mass of ethanol burns is used to heat a known mass of water; from the temperature rise the enthalpy of combustion is calculated.

**Apparatus:** spirit burner (containing ethanol) with a cap, copper can (calorimeter), clamp and stand, measuring cylinder, thermometer ($0-100^\circ$C), electronic balance, stirrer, draught shield (heat shield), matches.

**Set-up:** the copper can is clamped above the spirit burner at a fixed height, with a draught shield around it to reduce heat loss, and the thermometer dips into the water in the can.

**Procedure:**

1. Using the measuring cylinder, put a known volume (for example 200 cm$^3$) of water in the copper can. Its mass is 200 g (density of water = 1 g/cm$^3$).
2. Weigh the spirit burner with its cap and the ethanol in it. Record this as the **initial mass** of the burner.
3. Stir the water and record its **initial temperature**.
4. Place the burner under the can, light the wick, and stir the water continuously with the thermometer or stirrer.
5. When the temperature has risen by about $20-25^\circ$C, put out the flame with the cap and immediately record the **highest temperature** of the water.
6. Reweigh the burner with its cap and record the **final mass**.
7. Repeat the experiment and take the average.

**Results (data collected):**

| Quantity | Symbol / value |
|---|---|
| Volume (mass) of water | 200 cm$^3$ (200 g) |
| Initial temperature of water | $T_1$ |
| Final temperature of water | $T_2$ |
| Mass of burner before | $m_1$ |
| Mass of burner after | $m_2$ |

Mass of ethanol burnt $= m_1 - m_2$. Temperature rise $\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$.

**Use of the data:** heat gained by water $Q = m_{\text{water}} \times c \times \Delta T$ (with $c = 4.2\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,^\circ C^{-1}}$); number of moles of ethanol $= \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{46}$; enthalpy of combustion $\Delta H_c = -\dfrac{Q}{\text{moles of ethanol}}$ (negative, because heat is released).

**Source of error:** heat loss to the surroundings and to the can, and incomplete combustion, so the experimental value is lower in magnitude than the true value.

questions.enonce_markdown: In one of such experiments, when 0.4 g of ethanol was burnt, the temperature of 200 cm$^3$ of water was raised from $25.2^\circ$C to $50.0^\circ$C. Determine the enthalpy of combustion. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Mass of water $= 200\ \mathrm{g}$ (density 1 g/cm$^3$). Temperature rise $\Delta T = 50.0 - 25.2 = 24.8^\circ$C.

Heat gained by the water: $Q = mc\Delta T = 200 \times 4.2 \times 24.8 = 20832\ \mathrm{J} = 20.83\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

Molar mass of ethanol, $\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}$: $2(12.0) + 6(1.0) + 16.0 = 46\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

Moles of ethanol burnt: $n = \dfrac{0.4}{46} = 0.00870\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Enthalpy of combustion for 1 mole: $\Delta H_c = -\dfrac{20.83}{0.00870} = -2396\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

$\Delta H_c \approx \mathbf{-2.40\times10^{3}\ kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ (the negative sign shows the reaction is exothermic). The value follows directly from the data given in the question; it is larger than the accepted value (about $-1367$ kJ/mol), which does not change the working expected here.
